title: Sharpening a bench chisel on a whetstone
subtitle: Flatten the back, establish a primary bevel, and hone a sharp secondary bevel on a bench chisel using oil or water sharpening stones
excerpt: How to sharpen a bevel-edge bench chisel on a sharpening stone. Covers flattening the back, grinding or establishing the primary bevel, honing the secondary bevel on progressively finer stones, and stropping to a final edge.
sourceNotes: Newey and Drage, Practical Carpentry and Joinery (referenced, not reproduced). Carpentry for Boys (1914, public domain). Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics (referenced, not reproduced).

glossaryTerms.definition: The main ground bevel of a chisel, set at 25 degrees. This is the long flat ramp from the shoulder of the blade to just behind the cutting edge. The primary bevel is rarely touched once set; re-grinding is needed only when the chisel is chipped or very dull.

A small bevel honed at 30 degrees on top of the primary bevel. Only a few millimetres wide. This is the actual cutting edge. Honing only the secondary bevel means working a much smaller area, making the sharpening process faster.

A flat abrasive stone used for sharpening edged tools. Oil stones (Arkansas, India) use oil as a lubricant; water stones (Japanese synthetic stones) use water. Both cut steel; water stones cut faster and are graded finer. A combination stone (coarse one side, fine the other) is adequate for most workshop needs.

content.text: A bench chisel is sharpened by establishing the correct bevel angle at the cutting edge and polishing that angle to a fine enough finish to cut cleanly. The
whetstone
does the work. What makes sharpening hard is maintaining a consistent angle; what makes it fast is working on only the
secondary bevel
, not the full
primary bevel
each time.
Flatten the back of the chisel

Hold the chisel flat (bevel side up) on the coarse stone and work the back with circular strokes until the full width of the back near the cutting edge is showing a consistent scratch pattern. The back must be flat, or no sharpening of the bevel will produce a good edge. Move to the fine stone and polish the back to a mirror finish near the tip. This step is done once on a new chisel and only repeated if the chisel rusts or is damaged.
Establish the primary bevel

The primary bevel should be at 25 degrees. Place the chisel bevel-down on the coarse stone and tilt it until the whole bevel face rests flat. This is the primary angle; feel for the moment when the bevel rests with no rocking. Hone until a consistent scratch pattern covers the whole bevel. This step is for re-grinding a damaged edge. A honing guide clipped to the blade keeps the angle consistent if you do not yet have the feel for free-hand honing.
Hone the secondary bevel

Place the chisel bevel-down on the fine stone and raise the heel by an extra 5 degrees (to approximately 30 degrees). This lifts the bevel so only the tip zone contacts the stone. Work forward and back with light pressure. The secondary bevel is only 1-2 mm wide; a dozen firm strokes is enough on a fine stone. A burr (a thin wire edge) will form on the back of the blade. Feel for it with a finger pad.
Remove the burr and test the edge

Lay the chisel back flat on the fine stone and make two or three light strokes to remove the burr from the back. Alternate: a single light stroke on the bevel, one flat stroke on the back, until the burr is gone. Test on the end grain of a piece of softwood: a sharp chisel cuts with almost no pressure and leaves a clean, burnished surface. A dull chisel tears and needs more work on the stone.
What it looks like when it is right

The secondary bevel is a bright, mirror-polished strip at the tip. The back is flat and shiny near the edge. The tool shaves end grain cleanly with no pressure. Holding the edge up to a raking light, no bright white reflection should be visible along the cutting edge: a visible white line means a flat spot that is not sharp.
Common mistakes
Rocking the chisel during the honing stroke rounds the bevel and prevents a clean secondary bevel forming. Lock the wrists; do not bend the hands during the stroke.
Using a stone that is dished in the middle gives a convex bevel. Flatten the stone periodically on a lapping plate or a sheet of silicon-carbide paper on a flat surface.
Skipping the burr-removal step leaves a fragile wire edge that folds over on the first cut. Always flatten the back after honing the bevel.
